evidence: addTask: validates the project and assignee exist through repository ports, calls Task.create with a generated id and the clock time, then calls tasks.save. This is use-case orchestration.
assignTask and markTaskDone pass the state change to the domain entity (task.assignTo, task.markDone) and then save. The business rules stay in the domain.
requireProject and requireUser throw domain errors (NotFoundError, ValidationError) after lookups through injected ports. There is no persistence implementation.
The file has no HTTP, request/response, database or framework code. The infrastructure files http-app.ts and server.ts import this service, so transport lives outside it.
Minor: addTask sets the default status "todo" (command.status ?? "todo"). This could belong in the domain factory, but it is too small to count as a misplaced responsibility.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: TaskService is a standard application service. It coordinates use cases such as addTask, getTask, assignTask, markTaskDone and listTasks. It works only through repository, id-generator and clock ports that are declared in the domain. It builds tasks with the domain factory Task.create and leaves state changes to domain entity methods (task.assignTo, task.markDone). The checks that a project or user exists are cross-aggregate lookups through repository ports, which is normal use-case orchestration and not a core business rule. The file has no persistence code (no SQL, ORM or file I/O), no transport or HTTP handling, and no framework coupling. The one borderline item is the default status "todo" in addTask, a small policy that could live in the domain factory. It is too minor to count as a misplaced responsibility.
